name: Haa valley farmhouse homestays
summary: Registered family homestays in the villages of the Haa valley, in traditional rammed-earth and timber farmhouses. Simple rooms, wood stoves, home-cooked hoentoe and red rice, and often a hot stone bath. The best way to see rural western Bhutan on a budget.
body: Haa has more working farmhouse stays than most western valleys, partly because there are few hotels and partly because the district has promoted homestays. Houses are two or three storeys, with storage and sometimes animals below, family rooms above and an altar room at the top. Guest rooms have mattresses or beds, heavy quilts and a wood stove or electric heater; bathrooms are shared or simple attached, with hot water from a geyser or bucket.

Meals are eaten with the family: buckwheat hoentoe, red rice, datshi stews, greens and butter tea. Your licensed operator books the house, since homestays must be registered for tourists, and your guide stays nearby. Expect cockerels at dawn and village dogs at night. We do not name individual houses; operators rotate bookings across registered families.
why: One of the cheapest certified ways to sleep in Bhutan
Home cooking, including Haa's buckwheat hoentoe
Quiet valley with few tourists
price_band: ₹2,000–3,500 per person with dinner and breakfast (indicative)

faqs.q: Do Haa homestays have attached bathrooms?
faqs.a: Some do, many do not. Expect simple bathrooms, often shared, with hot water from a geyser or heated buckets. Ask your operator to choose a house with an attached bathroom if it matters to you.

faqs.q: Can I book a Haa homestay directly?
faqs.a: Tourists must use registered accommodation and travel with a licensed guide, so bookings normally go through your operator. Indian travellers can ask their operator for a specific village. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is a hot stone bath included?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most families charge about ₹800–1,500 for a hot stone bath, which takes a few hours to prepare, so ask in the morning.

name: Phobjikha valley farmhouse stays
summary: Registered farmhouse stays scattered around the Phobjikha valley floor and Gangtey village, a short walk from the crane marsh. Wood stoves, potato and buckwheat cooking and hot stone baths, at a fraction of the valley's lodge prices.
body: Phobjikha has a handful of luxury lodges, but most of the valley's beds are in farmhouses. Families who farm potatoes, turnips and buckwheat have converted one or two rooms for guests. Rooms are plain, with thick quilts and a bukhari stove; at 3,000 m, December nights fall to about −5 °C, so warmth matters more than decor. Bathrooms range from shared to simple attached.

Evenings are spent by the kitchen fire with kewa datshi, red rice and khuli. Many homes offer a hot stone bath. In crane season, mid-November to January, some houses are within sight of the marsh. Book early for the Black-necked Crane Festival on 11 November, when the valley fills. Your licensed operator books registered houses.
why: Sleep a short walk from the crane marsh
Hot stone baths and wood-stove kitchens
Far cheaper than the valley's lodges
price_band: ₹2,000–3,500 per person with dinner and breakfast (indicative)

faqs.q: Are Phobjikha farmhouses warm in winter?
faqs.a: Rooms have wood stoves or heaters and thick quilts, but corridors and bathrooms are cold. Bring thermals, a warm hat and socks for night. The valley drops to about −5 °C in December.

faqs.q: Can I see cranes from a homestay?
faqs.a: From some houses on the valley edge, yes, especially early morning. For closer and guided viewing, go to the RSPN crane centre viewpoints.

faqs.q: Is electricity reliable in Phobjikha?
faqs.a: The valley is on the national grid via underground cable, laid to protect the cranes. Short power cuts happen; carry a torch and a power bank.

name: Swiss Guest House, Jakar
summary: A farmhouse-style guesthouse on a hillside a few minutes above Jakar, one of Bumthang's first places for foreign travellers, open since the early 1980s. Wood-panelled rooms with stoves, apple orchards and a kitchen known for Swiss dishes alongside Bhutanese food.
body: The Swiss Guest House sits at Karsumphe, a short drive above Jakar, in a traditional farmhouse setting with orchards around it. Rooms are wood-panelled, with en-suite bathrooms and wood-burning stoves for Bumthang's cold nights. It has hosted travellers since the early 1980s and is linked to the Swiss community whose development work in Bumthang also left a cheese factory and a brewery.

The kitchen serves Bhutanese meals and Swiss dishes such as fondue and rösti, using Bumthang cheese. The bar serves Red Panda wheat beer from Jakar. It is simpler than Bumthang's luxury lodges but more characterful than most town hotels, and good value for comfort-minded saver travellers. Confirm current rates with your operator.
why: Wood stoves and orchard setting above Jakar
Swiss and Bhutanese cooking with Bumthang cheese
Long-running, well-known among Bhutan travellers
price_band: ₹3,500–6,500 a night for a double with breakfast (indicative)

faqs.q: Why is it called the Swiss Guest House?
faqs.a: It grew out of Bumthang's long Swiss connection, the same development work that set up the valley's cheese and beer production. The kitchen still serves Swiss dishes such as fondue alongside Bhutanese meals.

faqs.q: How far is the Swiss Guest House from Jakar?
faqs.a: A few minutes by car up the hillside at Karsumphe, above Jakar town. You can walk down to town in about 20–30 minutes.

faqs.q: Are rooms heated?
faqs.a: Yes, rooms have wood-burning stoves, and staff light them in the evening. Bumthang nights are near freezing in autumn and below in winter.

name: Hotel Druk, Thimphu
image_query: Hotel Druk Thimphu Clock Tower Square
summary: A long-running city hotel on Clock Tower Square in central Thimphu, open since 1985. Spacious rooms, a restaurant, bar and spa, and a location that lets you walk to Norzin Lam, the weekend market and the Memorial Chorten.
body: Hotel Druk overlooks Clock Tower Square, a few minutes' walk from Norzin Lam and about 10 minutes on foot from the Memorial Chorten. It has operated since 1985 and is one of Thimphu's established comfort hotels, with large rooms mixing classic and modern Bhutanese style, a restaurant serving Bhutanese, Indian and continental food, a bar and a spa.

For comfort travellers the location is the point: you can walk out in the evening to cafes, the square and the handicraft shops without your vehicle. Rooms facing the square are livelier; ask for a quieter side if you sleep lightly. It suits families and couples who want a central base for two nights between Paro and Punakha.
why: Central location on Clock Tower Square
Established since 1985 with spacious rooms
Walk to Norzin Lam, cafes and the weekend market
price_band: ₹8,000–14,000 a night for a double with breakfast (indicative)

faqs.q: Where is Hotel Druk in Thimphu?
faqs.a: On Clock Tower Square in the city centre, a short walk from Norzin Lam, the main street, and about 10 minutes on foot from the Memorial Chorten.

faqs.q: Is Hotel Druk good for families?
faqs.a: Yes. Rooms are spacious, the restaurant handles Indian and Bhutanese meals and the central location means short walks for children. Ask for interconnecting rooms in advance.

faqs.q: Is Hotel Druk noisy?
faqs.a: Rooms facing Clock Tower Square can hear evening events and traffic. Thimphu is quiet by Indian city standards, but light sleepers should ask for a rear-facing room.

name: Zhiwa Ling Heritage, Paro
summary: A hand-built Bhutanese hotel at Satsam Chorten in the Paro valley, opened in 2005 after five years of work by Bhutanese artisans. Carved and painted woodwork throughout, and a temple inside built with old timbers from Gangtey Goenpa.
body: Zhiwa Ling sits at Satsam Chorten, about 5 minutes by car from Kyichu Lhakhang and a short drive from Rinpung Dzong and the Taktsang trailhead. It was built over five years by Bhutanese carpenters, carvers and painters and opened in 2005 as the first Bhutanese-owned hotel of its class. Its about 45 rooms and suites are heavy with carved timber and painted motifs.

Inside, a temple on the second floor uses timbers taken from Gangtey Goenpa during that monastery's restoration, said to be some 450 years old. The hotel has a restaurant, bar, indoor pool, spa and hot stone baths. It sits at the top of our mid tier on price, and is the stay for travellers who want Bhutanese craft rather than international styling.
why: Built by Bhutanese artisans, opened 2005
Temple inside with old Gangtey Goenpa timbers
Close to Kyichu Lhakhang and the Taktsang trailhead
price_band: ₹14,000–25,000 a night for a double with breakfast (indicative)

faqs.q: What makes Zhiwa Ling special?
faqs.a: It was hand-built by Bhutanese artisans over five years and opened in 2005, with carved and painted woodwork throughout and a temple inside that uses old timbers from Gangtey Goenpa.

faqs.q: How far is Zhiwa Ling from Tiger's Nest?
faqs.a: The Taktsang trailhead is a short drive up the valley, roughly 15–20 minutes. Kyichu Lhakhang is about 5 minutes away.

faqs.q: Does Zhiwa Ling have a hot stone bath?
faqs.a: Yes, the hotel offers traditional hot stone baths and spa treatments, booked in advance. Ask your operator to reserve one for the evening after your Taktsang hike.

name: Dewachen Hotel, Gangtey
summary: A 16-room lodge in traditional Bhutanese style at the edge of the Phobjikha valley, near Gangtey village and the Black Mountains. Wood-burning stoves in every room, a restaurant with valley views and a hot stone bath.
body: Dewachen stands on the edge of the Phobjikha valley near Gangtey, with painted carved-wood eaves and whitewashed walls in high Bhutanese style. Its 16 rooms, mostly twins with a few doubles, have en-suite bathrooms and wood-burning stoves; staff add hot water bottles on cold nights, which in December reach about −5 °C.

The restaurant is built around a central stove with large windows over the valley, so you can watch for cranes over breakfast in season. There is a bar, a games room and a hot stone bath. Staff can arrange walks on the Gangtey nature trail, horse riding and visits to the crane centre. It is the comfort pick for crane season; book months ahead for November.
why: Valley views over the crane marsh
Wood stoves in every room
Hot stone bath and help with crane walks
price_band: ₹7,000–12,000 a night for a double with meals (indicative)

faqs.q: Can I see cranes from Dewachen Hotel?
faqs.a: In crane season, from late October to February, the restaurant windows look over the valley, and birds are often visible in the distance. For closer viewing, walk to the RSPN viewpoints.

faqs.q: Is Dewachen heated?
faqs.a: Rooms have wood-burning stoves and staff provide hot water bottles. Bathrooms and corridors are cooler, so pack warm layers.

faqs.q: How far ahead should I book for the crane festival?
faqs.a: At least three to four months. The festival on 11 November and the weeks around it fill Phobjikha's limited rooms quickly.

name: Amankora
summary: Aman's circuit of five lodges in Paro, Thimphu, Punakha, Gangtey and Bumthang, designed to be travelled in sequence. Rammed-earth walls, pine and stone, full board and private guides, each lodge sited in a quiet corner of its valley.
body: Amankora is one hotel spread across five lodges: Paro, in blue pine forest near the ruins of Drukgyel Dzong; Thimphu, in forest near Dechencholing Palace at the north end of the valley; Punakha, reached by a suspension bridge over the river and through orange orchards; Gangtey, above the Phobjikha marsh; and Bumthang, beside the Wangdue Chhoeling Palace in Jakar. Guests move between them by road with an Aman guide.

The design is consistent: rammed-earth walls, timber, wood-burning stoves and large windows facing each valley. Stays are usually sold on a full-board basis with guiding and touring, and each lodge offers spa treatments and hot stone baths. It is the most expensive way to see Bhutan, and the one with the least logistics to think about. Rates vary by season; confirm with Aman or your operator.
why: Five lodges designed as one lodge-to-lodge journey
Quiet sites in Paro, Thimphu, Punakha, Gangtey and Bumthang
Full board, private guiding and spa in each valley
price_band: From about ₹1,50,000 a night for a suite, full board (indicative)

faqs.q: How many Amankora lodges are there?
faqs.a: Five: Paro, Thimphu, Punakha, Gangtey (Phobjikha) and Bumthang. Most guests combine three to five of them on a 6–12 night journey.

faqs.q: Is Amankora all-inclusive?
faqs.a: Amankora stays are generally sold with meals, guiding and touring included, but the exact inclusions, SDF and drinks policy vary by package. Confirm what is included before booking.

faqs.q: Do I still pay SDF at Amankora?
faqs.a: Yes. The Sustainable Development Fee is charged by the government on every tourist night, regardless of hotel: ₹1,200 for Indians and USD 100 for most other nationalities as we understand it. Check current status before you travel.

name: Six Senses Bhutan
image_query: Six Senses Punakha lodge rice fields
summary: Five lodges in Thimphu, Paro, Punakha, Gangtey and Bumthang, with 82 suites and villas in all, designed for a multi-valley journey. Punakha's lodge sits among rice terraces above the Mo Chhu; each has its own spa and character.
body: Six Senses Bhutan is a circuit of five lodges. Thimphu, on a ridge above the city, has the largest spa and a glass-walled pool. Punakha is the warmest, a farmhouse-style lodge among rice terraces. Gangtey looks over the Phobjikha valley and its wintering cranes. Bumthang is the most easterly, set in a pine forest. Paro, built around old stone ruins, is the base for the Taktsang hike.

Between them the lodges hold 82 suites and villas. Guests usually travel a set route with a dedicated host, though stays at single lodges are possible. Each lodge offers wellness programmes, hot stone baths and food using local produce. Rates vary by season and package; confirm inclusions and SDF treatment with Six Senses or your operator.
why: Five lodges, including a warm rice-terrace lodge in Punakha
Strong wellness and spa programmes
Small scale: 82 keys across the whole circuit
price_band: From about ₹1,20,000 a night for a suite (indicative)

faqs.q: Where are the Six Senses lodges in Bhutan?
faqs.a: Thimphu, Paro, Punakha, Gangtey (Phobjikha) and Bumthang. The full circuit is often sold as a journey of around 10–12 nights.

faqs.q: Which Six Senses lodge is best for families?
faqs.a: Punakha is the warmest and lowest, at about 1,200 m in the valley, with gentle walks and river activities nearby. Ask about villa options for families.

faqs.q: Can I stay at just one Six Senses lodge?
faqs.a: Yes, single-lodge stays are possible, and many guests combine one or two lodges with other hotels. Confirm minimum stays and rates with the hotel or your operator.

name: COMO Uma Paro
summary: A 29-key resort on a pine-covered hill above Paro town, on a 37-acre estate a short drive from the airport. Rooms, suites and private villas, a COMO Shambhala spa with hot stone bathhouses, and a well-regarded restaurant.
body: Uma Paro sits on a hill above Paro, within a short drive of the airport, Rinpung Dzong and the Taktsang trailhead. Its 20 rooms and suites and nine one- and two-bedroom villas mix clean contemporary design with Bhutanese craft. The estate covers about 37 acres of pine forest, with walking paths and views over the Paro valley.

The COMO Shambhala spa has two private hot stone bathhouses, an indoor pool and a gym, and runs yoga and wellness programmes. The restaurant serves Bhutanese and international food. COMO also runs Uma Punakha on the Mo Chhu, which many guests combine with Paro. Rates vary by room type and season; confirm with COMO or your operator.
why: Hilltop estate minutes from Paro airport
Private villas and COMO Shambhala spa
Easy base for Taktsang and the Haa day trip
price_band: From about ₹55,000 a night for a double (indicative)

faqs.q: How far is COMO Uma Paro from the airport?
faqs.a: A short drive, typically 15–20 minutes, up the hill above Paro town. Your guide or the hotel can arrange the transfer.

faqs.q: Does Uma Paro have villas?
faqs.a: Yes, nine one- and two-bedroom private villas, some with butler service, alongside 20 rooms and suites. Villas suit families and honeymooners.

faqs.q: Can I combine Uma Paro with Uma Punakha?
faqs.a: Yes. COMO runs both, and a Paro–Punakha combination is a common 6–8 night signature itinerary, with Thimphu on the way.
